subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: The pituitary releases TSH to stimulate thyroid hormone production, while thyroid hormones feedback to suppress TRH and TSH. Dysregulation leads to hypo‑ or hyperthyroidism with systemic effects.

sections.p: The hypothalamus, pituitary, and thyroid form a hormonal loop that controls metabolism, growth, and energy balance. The pituitary’s TSH is the key driver of thyroid hormone synthesis.

TRH binds pituitary receptors, stimulating TSH secretion. TSH binds thyroid cells, activating deiodinases and thyroglobulin synthesis. T3/T4 circulate, bind nuclear receptors, and exert metabolic effects.

t.b: Elevated TSH suggests primary hypothyroidism; low TSH suggests hyperthyroidism or central suppression.
Low free T4 with high TSH indicates primary hypothyroidism; high free T4 with low TSH indicates hyperthyroidism.
Low TRH with low TSH suggests central hypothyroidism.

sections.p: Negative feedback: high T3/T4 suppress TRH and TSH. Deiodinase activity adjusts peripheral T3/T4 ratios. Stress, illness, and medications can blunt this loop.

t.b: Failure to suppress TSH after TRH indicates pituitary resistance.

sections.p: Pituitary disorders (adenomas, hypopituitarism) alter TSH release. Thyroid disorders (autoimmune, iodine deficiency, nodules) change hormone production. Central vs. primary causes differ in presentation.

t.b: Low TSH with low free T4 = central; high TSH with low free T4 = primary.

sections.p: Thyroid dysfunction affects cardiovascular, neurocognitive, and metabolic health. In low‑resource settings, iodine deficiency and infections (TB, HIV) exacerbate disease burden.
Remember the order of the axis, feedback logic, and that TSH is the best screen. Distinguish central from primary by TSH and free T4 patterns.
b: TSH high + free T4 low = primary hypothyroidism
TSH low + free T4 high = hyperthyroidism

t.b: High TSH + low free T4 = primary hypothyroidism; low TSH + high free T4 = hyperthyroidism.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden neurological deficits in pituitary apoplexy

faq.a: Yes, acute stress can transiently raise TSH, but chronic illness often lowers it.

faq.q: Is iodine deficiency common in low‑resource areas?
faq.a: Yes, especially where iodized salt is unavailable; it leads to goitre and hypothyroidism.
Yes, steroids, amiodarone, and antiepileptics can alter TSH and free T4 levels.

exam: Explain how TSH regulates thyroid hormone synthesis and why TSH is the preferred screening test.
Differentiate primary hypothyroidism from central hypothyroidism using TSH and free T4 values.
Describe the impact of iodine deficiency on thyroid function and public health strategies to prevent it.
